title: AUD U2·W4 — Audit Reports & Communications (CPA Core)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — the report is the product

Every procedure exists to support one deliverable: the auditor's report. The opinion expressed there is what users rely on, so the rules for which opinion to issue, and what to add to or change in the report, are the payoff of the whole audit. This week covers the standard report, the modified opinions, the extra paragraphs, and the communications that surround the report.

The unmodified opinion and report structure

When the statements are fairly presented in accordance with the framework, the auditor issues an unmodified (nonissuer) or unqualified (issuer) opinion. The report has a defined structure: a title referencing independence, the addressee, an Opinion section (now placed first), a Basis for Opinion section (stating independence and that sufficient appropriate evidence was obtained), the responsibilities of management (including going-concern evaluation), the auditor's responsibilities (reasonable assurance, materiality, professional skepticism), and the firm's signature, city, and date. The report date is no earlier than the date the auditor obtained sufficient appropriate evidence.

When to modify the opinion

Two problems force a modification, and their severity sets the type. A GAAP departure (a misstatement) or a scope limitation (unable to obtain sufficient evidence) leads to a qualified opinion when the matter is material but not pervasive. When the matter is material AND pervasive, a GAAP departure yields an adverse opinion (the statements are not fairly presented) and a scope limitation yields a disclaimer (the auditor expresses no opinion). The two-by-two — issue type by pervasiveness — is the single most tested reporting concept.

Emphasis-of-matter and other-matter paragraphs

Sometimes the opinion is unmodified but the auditor adds a paragraph. An emphasis-of-matter (EOM) paragraph highlights something properly presented in the statements that is fundamental to users' understanding — a major catastrophe, a significant related-party transaction, or a justified change in accounting principle. An other-matter (OM) paragraph addresses something not in the statements but relevant to the audit or report — for example, prior-period statements audited by a predecessor. Neither changes the opinion; they direct the reader's attention.

Going concern

Management must evaluate whether there is substantial doubt about the entity's ability to continue as a going concern for a reasonable period (generally one year). If substantial doubt exists but is adequately disclosed, the auditor typically issues an unmodified opinion with a separate going-concern section (an emphasis-of-matter). If the disclosure is inadequate, it becomes a GAAP departure (qualified or adverse). A severe, multiple-uncertainty situation can support a disclaimer. The auditor evaluates management's plans to mitigate the doubt before concluding.

Critical and key audit matters

For a PCAOB issuer audit, the report communicates critical audit matters (CAMs) — the matters arising from the audit that involved especially challenging, subjective, or complex auditor judgment and that relate to material accounts or disclosures. The AU-C/IAASB analogue, key audit matters (KAMs), applies to nonissuer and international reporting and is communicated when the auditor is engaged or required to do so. Neither CAMs nor KAMs modify the opinion; both simply give users insight into where the audit focused, increasing the report's informational value without changing the bottom-line conclusion.

Subsequent events and subsequently discovered facts

Events after the balance-sheet date but before the report is issued get two treatments (from FAR): a Type I (recognized) event provides evidence about conditions existing at the balance-sheet date and adjusts the statements; a Type II (nonrecognized) event reflects new conditions and is disclosed. If the auditor learns of facts after the report is issued that, had they been known, would have changed the report, the auditor investigates and, if the statements are affected and people are relying on them, ensures the issue is addressed (revised statements or notification). The management representation letter, dated as of the report date, documents management's assertions and is required audit evidence.

Other engagements and communications

Not every engagement is an audit. A review (SSARS for nonissuers) gives limited assurance via inquiry and analytics; a compilation gives no assurance. Statements may be prepared under a special-purpose framework (cash, tax, or regulatory basis), which the report describes and which uses an emphasis-of-matter paragraph. In a group audit, the group auditor decides whether to reference a component auditor (dividing responsibility) or to take full responsibility. Throughout, the auditor must communicate with those charged with governance — significant findings, significant deficiencies and material weaknesses (in writing), disagreements with management, and the auditor's responsibilities — closing the loop the audit opened.

Comparative statements, consistency, and other information

Reports rarely cover a single year. With comparative statements, the auditor's opinion covers all periods presented; if a predecessor audited a prior year, either the predecessor reissues its report or the successor adds an other-matter paragraph describing the prior audit. A change in accounting principle that is properly applied and disclosed warrants an emphasis-of-matter paragraph on consistency — the opinion stays unmodified. The auditor also reads the other information in an annual report (management's discussion, the chair's letter) for material inconsistencies with the audited statements; a refusal by management to correct a material inconsistency can require the auditor to describe it or take further action.

Reporting on internal control and the integrated audit

For an issuer, the auditor of an accelerated or large accelerated filer also reports on the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting in an integrated audit (the §404(b) attestation from AUD Unit 1), and a material weakness there produces an adverse opinion on ICFR even when the financial-statement opinion is unmodified. For nonissuers, an examination of internal control is a separate attestation engagement. The thread tying the unit together is that the report is a calibrated statement: the opinion, the added paragraphs, the ICFR conclusion, and the communications each carry a precise meaning, and the auditor's craft is choosing exactly the right combination for what the evidence showed.

CMA bridge

AUD Unit 1's control deficiencies and Unit 2's evidence all converge here, in the opinion. The going-concern and subsequent-event rules tie back to FAR; the report is where the auditor translates everything learned about MBG's statements into the single conclusion users act on — fairly presented, qualified, adverse, or no opinion at all.

Practice and recap

  1. Know the unmodified report structure (Opinion first, then Basis, responsibilities, signature/date).
  2. Choose the modification by issue and pervasiveness: qualified (material, not pervasive); adverse (GAAP departure, pervasive); disclaimer (scope limitation, pervasive).
  3. Add an EOM (something properly in the statements) or OM (something outside them); report going concern as an EOM when disclosure is adequate; communicate CAMs in PCAOB issuer reports (KAMs only when engaged/required under nonissuer/international standards).
  4. Apply Type I (adjust) vs Type II (disclose) subsequent events; obtain the management representation letter; communicate with those charged with governance.

Recap: the unmodified report leads with the opinion; a material-but-not-pervasive problem yields a qualified opinion, a pervasive GAAP departure an adverse opinion, and a pervasive scope limitation a disclaimer; emphasis-of-matter and going-concern paragraphs flag matters without changing the opinion; critical audit matters (CAMs) inform PCAOB issuer readers (KAMs under nonissuer/international standards when required); and subsequent-event, representation-letter, and governance-communication rules surround the report the audit produces. Comparative statements carry the opinion across all periods presented, a properly disclosed change in principle draws a consistency emphasis-of-matter, and for an issuer the integrated audit adds an ICFR opinion that turns adverse on a material weakness — each element a precisely calibrated signal to the user.

flashcards.back: Title (independence), addressee, Opinion section FIRST, Basis for Opinion, management's responsibilities, auditor's responsibilities, signature/city/date.
A GAAP departure or scope limitation that is material but NOT pervasive.
Adverse = pervasive GAAP departure (statements not fairly presented); disclaimer = pervasive scope limitation (no opinion expressed).
EOM = something properly presented IN the statements that is fundamental; OM = something relevant but NOT in the statements. Neither changes the opinion.
Unmodified opinion with a separate going-concern section (emphasis-of-matter); inadequate disclosure → GAAP departure (qualified/adverse).

PCAOB issuer reports communicate CRITICAL audit matters (CAMs); KEY audit matters (KAMs) are the AU-C/IAASB nonissuer/international concept, communicated when engaged/required. Neither modifies the opinion.

flashcards.front: Type I vs Type II subsequent events
flashcards.back: Type I (conditions existing at year-end) → adjust; Type II (new conditions after year-end) → disclose.
Audit = reasonable assurance (opinion); review = limited (negative) assurance; compilation = no assurance.

questions.q: A GAAP departure that is material but NOT pervasive results in a(n):
questions.explain: Material-but-not-pervasive issues (departure or scope limitation) yield a qualified opinion.

questions.q: A scope limitation that is material AND pervasive results in a(n):
questions.explain: A pervasive scope limitation → disclaimer; a pervasive GAAP departure → adverse.

questions.q: A pervasive GAAP departure (statements not fairly presented) results in a(n):
questions.explain: A material and pervasive GAAP departure yields an adverse opinion.

questions.q: An emphasis-of-matter paragraph is used to highlight:
choices: A matter properly presented in the statements that is fundamental to users
questions.explain: EOM highlights something correctly presented in the statements; it does not change the opinion.

questions.q: When substantial going-concern doubt exists but is adequately disclosed, the auditor usually issues:
choices: An unmodified opinion with a going-concern (emphasis-of-matter) section
questions.explain: Adequate disclosure → unmodified opinion with a separate going-concern section; inadequate disclosure → qualified/adverse.

questions.q: A subsequent event providing evidence about conditions existing at the balance-sheet date is:
choices: A Type I event — adjust the statements
A Type II event — disclose only
questions.explain: Type I (recognized) events adjust the statements; Type II (nonrecognized) events are disclosed.
A review gives limited assurance via inquiry and analytics; an audit gives reasonable assurance; a compilation none.
